newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin says economy on right path.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin says economy on right path.

text.p: French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said on Thursday that deficit-reduction measures unveiled this week had put France on the right path without undermining economic growth.

"We have opted for a measured and balanced plan to put things right. Measured, because with a reduction of 32 billion francs, or 0.4 percent of gross domestic product, we return to the right track without undermining economic growth," he said in a speech announcing the creation of an independent council of economic analysis to advise the government.

He said the choice was balanced because a revenue shortfall estimated at 20 to 23 billion francs would be offset by 22 billion from a temporary corporate tax increase after several years in which corporate savings far exceeded investments.

Jospin said he was aware of the crucial role of business in generating growth and jobs. "What we are asking from them now will be compensated by the prospect of rapid monetary union, by the deadlines set in the (Maastricht) treaty, with interest rates kept low and rising household demand due to a policy favouring consumption," he said.
The speech marked Jospin's first comments on the deficit-reduction plan presented on Monday by Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn.

"These measures had the objective of correcting a trajectory that would have left us without any margin for manoeuvre and compromised structural reforms to control public spending that will be adopted in the autumn with the 1998 budget and welfare financing bill," he said.

Referring to the public and private sectors, Jospin said the government needed to be attentive to the state's financial interests and assets. "This could lead to different choices, depending on the sector, and will be neither the status quo nor systematic privatisation," he said.
He asked the 38-member council to consider, in addition to policy matters, broad issues such as the tax structure, charges and the impact on employment, and possible reform.

"I would like the council members to give me their views quickly on how they see the economic situation ... and the conditions that would allow us to reconcile strong growth and a more equitable distribution of the benefits of this growth," he said.
